questions.question: Which of the following correctly describes an antibonding molecular orbital?
options: It concentrates electron density between the two nuclei
It has a nodal plane between the nuclei and lies higher in energy than the parent atomic orbitals
It is formed by constructive overlap of the atomic orbitals
It lies lower in energy than the parent atomic orbitals and stabilises the molecule

solution.key_concept: Antibonding MOs come from destructive overlap. They have a node between the nuclei and lie higher in energy than the parent AOs.
steps: Destructive overlap cancels electron density between the nuclei, which creates a nodal plane there.
With no density between the nuclei, repulsion is not reduced, so the orbital lies above the parent AOs.
Electrons in it destabilise the molecule.
solution.final_answer: Option (2): It has a nodal plane between the nuclei and lies higher in energy than the parent atomic orbitals
solution.why_not_others: Options 1, 3 and 4 describe a bonding MO: electron density between the nuclei, constructive overlap and lower energy.
solution.common_trap: Mixing up the features of bonding and antibonding orbitals.
solution.time_saving_tip: An asterisk (*) means a node between the nuclei and higher energy.

questions.question: Which molecular orbital has a nodal plane containing the internuclear axis and also an additional node between the nuclei?

solution.key_concept: All pi MOs have a nodal plane containing the internuclear axis. $\pi^*$ orbitals also have an additional node between the nuclei.
steps: A nodal plane containing the internuclear axis is the mark of a pi orbital, so the choice is between $\pi 2p_x$ and $\pi^* 2p_x$.
An extra node between the nuclei is the mark of an antibonding orbital.
Only $\pi^* 2p_x$ has both features.
solution.final_answer: Option (2): $\pi^* 2p_x$
solution.why_not_others: $\sigma 2p_z$ is symmetrical about the axis and has no node between the nuclei. $\pi 2p_x$ has no node between the nuclei. $\sigma^* 2p_z$ has a node between the nuclei but is cylindrically symmetrical, so no nodal plane contains the axis.
solution.common_trap: Choosing $\sigma^* 2p_z$ because it is antibonding, while forgetting that sigma orbitals have no nodal plane containing the axis.

questions.question: When two atomic orbitals combine to form a bonding and an antibonding molecular orbital, which statement about their energies is correct?
options: The bonding MO is lowered by exactly the same amount as the antibonding MO is raised
The antibonding MO is raised slightly more than the bonding MO is lowered
The bonding MO is lowered more than the antibonding MO is raised
Both the bonding and antibonding MOs lie below the parent atomic orbitals

solution.key_concept: Energy splitting is unequal: the antibonding MO is destabilised slightly more than the bonding MO is stabilised.
steps: The bonding MO lies below the parent AOs.
The antibonding MO lies above the parent AOs.
The rise of the antibonding MO is slightly larger than the fall of the bonding MO.
solution.final_answer: Option (2): The antibonding MO is raised slightly more than the bonding MO is lowered
solution.why_not_others: Option 1 assumes symmetric splitting. Option 3 reverses the asymmetry. Option 4 is wrong because the antibonding MO lies above the parent AOs.
solution.common_trap: Assuming the splitting is symmetric.

questions.question: Given below are two statements: Assertion A and Reason R. Choose the correct answer.

statements.A: An electron placed in the $\sigma^* 1s$ orbital destabilises the molecule.
statements.R: The $\sigma^* 1s$ orbital is symmetrical about the internuclear axis.

options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

solution.key_concept: Antibonding electrons destabilise a molecule because the orbital lies higher in energy and has a node between the nuclei, not because of its symmetry.
steps: $\sigma^* 1s$ is an antibonding MO, higher in energy than the 1s AOs, so A is true.
All sigma MOs, bonding or antibonding, are symmetrical about the internuclear axis, so R is true.
The bonding $\sigma 1s$ orbital has the same symmetry, so symmetry cannot explain destabilisation. R does not explain A.
solution.final_answer: Option (2): Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
solution.why_not_others: R is a true statement, so options 3 and 4 fail. R does not explain A, so option 1 fails.
solution.common_trap: Accepting any true reason as the explanation.
solution.time_saving_tip: Ask whether R would also apply to the bonding orbital. If it would, it cannot explain destabilisation.

questions.question: Given below are two statements. Choose the most appropriate answer.

statements.I: The $\sigma 2p_z$ molecular orbital has a nodal plane containing the internuclear axis.
statements.II: Electrons in a bonding molecular orbital increase internuclear repulsion and therefore destabilise the molecule.

options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct

solution.key_concept: Sigma MOs are cylindrically symmetrical about the internuclear axis. Bonding MOs place electron density between the nuclei, which reduces repulsion and stabilises the molecule.
steps: A nodal plane containing the internuclear axis is a feature of pi MOs. $\sigma 2p_z$ is symmetrical about the axis, so Statement I is incorrect.
Bonding MOs concentrate electron density between the nuclei, which reduces repulsion and lowers energy, so Statement II is incorrect.
solution.final_answer: Option (2): Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
solution.why_not_others: Statement I describes a pi orbital, not a sigma orbital. Statement II describes the opposite of what bonding electrons do.
solution.common_trap: Assuming any p-derived MO must have a nodal plane along the axis.

questions.question: The highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO) of $N_2$ is:

solution.key_concept: For molecules with up to 14 electrons, s–p mixing raises $\sigma 2p_z$ above $\pi 2p$.
steps: The configuration of $N_2$ is $KK\,\sigma 2s^2\,\sigma^* 2s^2\,\pi 2p_x^2 = \pi 2p_y^2\,\sigma 2p_z^2$.
The last orbital filled is $\sigma 2p_z$, so it is the HOMO.
solution.final_answer: Option (4): $\sigma 2p_z$
solution.why_not_others: $\pi 2p$ is the HOMO only if the $O_2$-type order is wrongly applied. $\pi^* 2p$ is empty in $N_2$. $\sigma^* 2s$ lies lower than the 2p-derived MOs.
solution.common_trap: Using the $O_2$-type order, in which $\sigma 2p_z$ lies below $\pi 2p$.

questions.question: Which of the following homonuclear diatomic species has two unpaired electrons located in bonding $\pi 2p$ orbitals?

solution.key_concept: In $B_2$, the two electrons beyond $\sigma^* 2s$ occupy the degenerate $\pi 2p_x$ and $\pi 2p_y$ orbitals singly.
steps: $B_2$ has 10 electrons: $KK\,\sigma 2s^2\,\sigma^* 2s^2\,\pi 2p_x^1\,\pi 2p_y^1$.
By Hund's rule the two electrons stay unpaired in the bonding pi orbitals, so $B_2$ is paramagnetic.
solution.final_answer: Option (3): $B_2$
solution.why_not_others: $O_2$ also has two unpaired electrons, but they are in antibonding $\pi^*$ orbitals. $C_2$ and $N_2$ are diamagnetic.
solution.common_trap: Picking $O_2$ because it is the best-known paramagnetic molecule, without checking which orbitals hold the unpaired electrons.

questions.question: The spin-only magnetic moment of the $O_2$ molecule is approximately:

solution.key_concept: $O_2$ has two unpaired electrons in the $\pi^* 2p$ orbitals. Use $\mu = \sqrt{n(n+2)}$ BM.
steps: The configuration ends in $\pi^* 2p_x^1 = \pi^* 2p_y^1$, so n = 2.
$\mu = \sqrt{2(2+2)} = \sqrt{8} \approx 2.83$ BM.
solution.final_answer: Option (2): 2.83 BM
solution.why_not_others: 1.73 BM corresponds to n = 1, as in $O_2^+$ or $O_2^-$. 0 BM assumes $O_2$ is diamagnetic. 3.87 BM corresponds to n = 3.
solution.common_trap: Treating $O_2$ as diamagnetic, as a Lewis structure with all electrons paired suggests.

questions.question: Match List-I with List-II and choose the correct answer.

list_II.label: II
list_II.text: Paramagnetic, with two unpaired electrons in $\pi 2p$ orbitals

list_II.label: III
list_II.text: Diamagnetic; its double bond consists of two pi bonds

solution.key_concept: Apply the correct MO filling order to each molecule: the $N_2$-type order up to 14 electrons and the $O_2$-type order beyond that.
steps: $B_2$ has two unpaired electrons in $\pi 2p$, so A matches II.
$C_2$ has $\pi 2p^4$ with all electrons paired, giving two pi bonds, so B matches III.
$N_2$ has bond order 3 and its HOMO is $\sigma 2p_z$, so C matches IV.
$Ne_2$ has all MOs up to $\sigma^* 2p_z$ filled and bond order 0, so D matches I.
solution.final_answer: Option (3): A-II, B-III, C-IV, D-I
solution.why_not_others: Option 1 swaps $B_2$ and $C_2$. Option 2 swaps $N_2$ and $Ne_2$. Option 4 gives $B_2$ bond order 3.
solution.common_trap: Assuming $C_2$ has a sigma plus a pi bond, or that $B_2$ is diamagnetic.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about MO configurations of homonuclear diatomic molecules are correct?

statements.A: In $O_2$, the $\sigma 2p_z$ orbital lies below the $\pi 2p$ orbitals.
statements.B: In $N_2$, the $\sigma 2p_z$ orbital is filled after the $\pi 2p_x$ and $\pi 2p_y$ orbitals.
statements.C: $C_2$ contains one sigma bond and one pi bond in the simple MO picture.
statements.D: $O_2$ has two unpaired electrons in the $\pi^* 2p$ orbitals.

options: A, B, C and D only

solution.key_concept: s–p mixing raises $\sigma 2p_z$ above $\pi 2p$ only up to $N_2$. $C_2$ has only pi bonds, and $F_2$ is diamagnetic.
steps: A is true: for $O_2$, $F_2$ and $Ne_2$, $\sigma 2p_z$ lies below $\pi 2p$.
B is true: the $N_2$ configuration is $\ldots\pi 2p^4\,\sigma 2p_z^2$.
C is false: $C_2$ has $\pi 2p^4$ as its outermost electrons, giving two pi bonds and no sigma bond.
D is true: $\pi^* 2p_x^1 = \pi^* 2p_y^1$.
E is false: $F_2$ has all electrons paired, so it is diamagnetic.
solution.final_answer: Option (1): A, B and D only
solution.why_not_others: Options 2 and 4 include the false statement C. Option 3 includes the false statement E and leaves out the true statement A.
solution.common_trap: Assuming every double bond is one sigma plus one pi bond, which is not true for $C_2$ in the MO picture.

questions.question: The bond order of the superoxide ion, $O_2^-$, is:

solution.key_concept: B.O. = $\frac{1}{2}(N_b - N_a)$. Adding an electron to an antibonding orbital lowers the bond order.
steps: $O_2$ has $N_b = 10$ and $N_a = 6$, so its bond order is 2.
$O_2^-$ adds one electron to $\pi^*$, so $N_a = 7$.
solution.final_answer: Option (1): 1.5
solution.why_not_others: 2.5 is the bond order of $O_2^+$. 2 is that of $O_2$. 1 is that of $O_2^{2-}$.
solution.common_trap: Placing the extra electron in a bonding orbital, which gives 2.5.
solution.time_saving_tip: Each electron added to $\pi^*$ lowers the bond order by 0.5.

questions.question: Among the following, the species with the longest O–O bond is:

solution.key_concept: Bond length is inversely related to bond order.
steps: The lowest bond order gives the longest bond, so $O_2^{2-}$ has the longest bond.
solution.why_not_others: $O_2^+$ has the highest bond order and the shortest bond. $O_2$ and $O_2^-$ have higher bond orders than $O_2^{2-}$.
solution.common_trap: Assuming a higher bond order means a longer bond.

questions.question: Which of the following species has the same bond order as $NO^+$?

solution.key_concept: Isoelectronic species have the same bond order. $N_2$, $CO$, $NO^+$ and $CN^-$ each have 14 electrons and a bond order of 3.
steps: $NO^+$ has 7 + 8 − 1 = 14 electrons, so its bond order is 3.
$CN^-$ has 6 + 7 + 1 = 14 electrons, so its bond order is also 3.
solution.final_answer: Option (3): $CN^-$
solution.why_not_others: $O_2$ has bond order 2. $N_2^+$ and $O_2^+$ each have bond order 2.5.
solution.common_trap: Choosing a cation such as $O_2^+$ just because $NO^+$ is also a cation.
solution.time_saving_tip: Count the total electrons. A 14-electron diatomic species has bond order 3.

questions.question: Given below are two statements: Assertion A and Reason R. Choose the correct answer.

statements.A: $H_2^+$ and $He_2^+$ are equally stable because both have a bond order of 0.5.
statements.R: Bond order is half the difference between the numbers of electrons in bonding and antibonding molecular orbitals.

options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

solution.key_concept: When bond orders are equal, the species with fewer antibonding electrons is more stable.
steps: Both species have bond order 0.5.
$H_2^+$ has no antibonding electrons, while $He_2^+$ has one, so $H_2^+$ is more stable. A is false.
R is the correct definition of bond order, so R is true.
solution.final_answer: Option (4): A is false but R is true
solution.why_not_others: A is false, so options 1, 2 and 3 are all ruled out.
solution.common_trap: Concluding equal stability from equal bond order.

questions.question: Given below are two statements. Choose the most appropriate answer.

statements.I: $N_2^-$ is more stable than $N_2^+$ because it contains more electrons.
statements.II: The bond enthalpy of $F_2$ is higher than that of $Cl_2$ because the F atom is smaller.

options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct

solution.key_concept: For equal bond orders, fewer antibonding electrons means greater stability. In small F atoms, lone pair repulsion weakens the F–F bond.
steps: $N_2^+$ and $N_2^-$ both have bond order 2.5.
$N_2^-$ has an extra antibonding electron, so $N_2^+$ is more stable. Statement I is incorrect.
The bond enthalpy of $F_2$ is lower than that of $Cl_2$ because of lone pair repulsion in the small F atoms. Statement II is incorrect.
solution.final_answer: Option (2): Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
solution.why_not_others: Each statement contradicts a fact in the notes, so no option that calls either statement correct can be right.
solution.common_trap: Assuming a smaller atom always forms a stronger bond, as with $F_2$.

questions.question: According to the electron sea model, the metallic bond is the attraction between:
options: neighbouring neutral atoms sharing localised electron pairs
lone pairs on adjacent metal atoms
positive kernels and the sea of delocalised mobile electrons

solution.key_concept: Metal atoms lose their valence electrons to become positive kernels, which sit in a sea of delocalised electrons.
steps: Each atom gives up its valence electrons and becomes a kernel at a fixed lattice point.
The attraction between the kernels and the mobile electrons is the metallic bond.
solution.final_answer: Option (4): positive kernels and the sea of delocalised mobile electrons
solution.why_not_others: Option 1 describes covalent bonding. Option 2 describes ionic bonding. Option 3 describes no recognised bond type.
solution.common_trap: Confusing metallic bonding with covalent or ionic bonding.

questions.question: Which property of metals is explained by the ability of layers of positive kernels to slide over one another without breaking the metallic bond?

solution.key_concept: The metallic bond is non-directional, so layers can shift while the electron sea keeps holding the kernels together.
steps: When kernel layers slide, the attraction to the electron sea is not lost.
The metal therefore deforms without breaking, which is malleability and ductility.
solution.final_answer: Option (4): Malleability and ductility
solution.why_not_others: Lustre comes from electrons absorbing and re-emitting light. Electrical and thermal conductivity come from mobile electrons, not from sliding layers.
solution.common_trap: Attributing every metallic property to the mobile electrons alone.

questions.question: Alkali metals are soft and have low melting points mainly because:
options: their metallic bonding involves d electrons and is very strong
they have few valence electrons and large atomic size, so their metallic bonding is weak
their metallic bond is directional and breaks easily
they have many valence electrons and small atomic size

solution.key_concept: Metallic bond strength increases with the number of valence electrons and decreases with atomic size.
steps: Alkali metals have only one valence electron each.
They are also the largest atoms in their periods.
Both factors make the metallic bonding weak, which gives softness and low melting points.
solution.final_answer: Option (2): they have few valence electrons and large atomic size, so their metallic bonding is weak
solution.why_not_others: Option 1 describes transition metals. Option 3 is wrong because the metallic bond is non-directional. Option 4 describes conditions that give strong metallic bonding.
solution.common_trap: Believing a larger atomic size strengthens metallic bonding.

questions.question: Match List-I with List-II and choose the correct answer.

list_I.label: D
list_I.text: High melting points of transition metals

list_II.label: I
list_II.text: Mobile delocalised electrons that move through the lattice

list_II.label: II
list_II.text: Electrons that absorb and re-emit light

list_II.label: III
list_II.text: Layers of kernels that slide without breaking bonds

list_II.label: IV
list_II.text: Strong metallic bonding involving d electrons

solution.key_concept: The electron sea model explains each metallic property through a specific feature.
steps: Conductivity comes from mobile electrons, so A matches I.
Lustre comes from electrons absorbing and re-emitting light, so B matches II.
Malleability comes from sliding layers of kernels, so C matches III.
Transition metals have high melting points because of strong d-electron metallic bonding, so D matches IV.
solution.final_answer: Option (1): A-I, B-II, C-III, D-IV
solution.why_not_others: Option 2 swaps conductivity and lustre. Option 3 swaps malleability and melting point. Option 4 swaps conductivity and malleability.
solution.common_trap: Linking lustre to electron mobility instead of light absorption and re-emission.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about metallic bonding are correct?

statements.B: Metallic bond strength increases with increasing atomic size.
statements.C: Positive kernels occupy fixed lattice points in a sea of delocalised electrons.
statements.D: Metallic bond strength increases with the number of valence electrons.
statements.E: In a metal, the kernels move freely while the electrons remain fixed at lattice points.

solution.key_concept: In the electron sea model, kernels are fixed and electrons are mobile. Bond strength rises with more valence electrons and falls with larger atomic size.
steps: A is true: the metallic bond is non-directional.
B is false: bond strength decreases as atomic size increases.
C is true: kernels sit at fixed lattice points in the electron sea.
D is true: more valence electrons give a stronger metallic bond.
E is false: it reverses the model, since the electrons are mobile and the kernels are fixed.
solution.final_answer: Option (2): A, C and D only
solution.why_not_others: Option 1 includes the false statement B. Option 3 includes the false statement E. Option 4 leaves out the true statement C.
solution.common_trap: Swapping the roles of the kernels and the electrons.
